data.title: Notice of application in foreclosure action
sentences: (1) In a foreclosure action, notice of every application made by the plaintiff must be served on each person who filed and served on the plaintiff a statement of defence, a demand for notice or a notice of address for service.
(2) A defendant or subsequent encumbrancer who is not required to be 26 Law Society of Alberta Code of Conduct, April 26, 2018, Article 5.1-1, Commentary Paragraphs 6 and 8.
(3) A defendant who is not required to be served under subrule
(1) must be served with notice of an application in a foreclosure action if the application is for personal judgment against that defendant.
(4) A person who is not required to be served under subrule
(1) must be served with notice of an application in a foreclosure action for an order for possession if the plaintiff seeks possession of secured property from that person.
(5) An offeror or tenderer who is not required to be served under subrule
(1) must be served with notice of an application in a foreclosure action if one or more offers or tenders have been made on secured property and the application is for one or more of the following:
(a) an order confirming sale to the plaintiff or another person
(b) an order for possession, but not a preservation order
(c) an order appointing a receiver and manager
(d) a foreclosure order. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.5 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*
info_notes: Rule 11.24 [Notice of address for service in foreclosure actions] specifies the persons who may file and serve on the plaintiff in a foreclosure action a notice of address for service in Alberta.

commentary.text:
This rule particularly applies to foreclosure actions as defined in the Rules, and mentioned earlier. If an application relates to a foreclosure action, notice in accordance with this rule must be given. There are many parties interested in the outcome of foreclosure actions and this rule attempts to capture notice to them. See Part 9, Division 5, for additional rules and commentary specifically relating to foreclosure actions.
Application for Personal Judgment – Notice required under rule 6.5(3) applies to circumstances where a damages claim exposes the mortgagors to personal liability in the context of a foreclosure proceeding. CIBC Mortgages Inc. v. Fasami, [2015] A.J. No. 486, 2015 ABQB 286 at para. 13 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).

data.title: Response and reply to application
data.text:
(1) If the respondent to an application intends to rely on an affidavit or other evidence when the application is heard or considered, the respondent must reply by serving on the applicant a copy of the affidavit or other evidence a reasonable time before the application is to be heard or considered.
(2) The applicant may respond by affidavit or other evidence to the respondent’s affidavit or other evidence but must (a) serve the affidavit or other evidence on the respondent a reasonable time before the application is to be heard, and (b) limit the response to replying to the respondent’s affidavit or other evidence.
(3) If either the respondent or applicant does not give the other reasonable notice, the Court may impose costs on the party who did not give reasonable notice, and the party who did not give reasonable notice is not entitled to rely on that party’s affidavit or other evidence unless the Court otherwise permits.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.6 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

commentary.text:
This rule deals with the timing of response evidence to applications.
The touchstone for response is “reasonable time”. What is reasonable depends upon the circumstances. Courts do not look fondly upon late-delivered evidence, and the late delivery of evidence in an application could be grounds to have that evidence struck or disregarded.
The rules do not require that the respondent to an application serve its affidavit evidence before cross-examining applicant witnesses.
Reasonable Time – This rule applies to both morning chambers and special chambers applications; a reasonable time before the application is to be heard or considered is generally not only a few days before the receiving party’s brief is due for a special chambers application.  Romantic Planet Vacations Inc. v. Hartman, [2015] A.J. No. 1295, 2015 ABQB 743 at para. 19 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). Providing the affidavit only a few days before an application is to be heard forces a possible rushed rebuttal affidavit from the applicant. Cross-examination on the respondent’s affidavit is usually not possible without an adjournment, and it frustrates the preparation of the applicant’s brief. Romantic Planet Vacations Inc. v. Hartman, [2015] A.J. No. 1295, 2015 ABQB 743 at para. 19 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).

data.title: How the Court considers applications
data.text:
(1) The Court may consider a filed application in one or more of the following ways:
(a) in person, with one, some or all of the parties present;
(b) by means of an electronic hearing if an electronic hearing is permitted under rule 6.10 ;
[Electronic hearings]
(c) by a process involving documents only.
(2) Applications may be decided by a judge or applications judge.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.9 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021);Alta. Reg.*

136/2022, s. 1(2) effective September 1,  to govern the use of remote hearings. These guidelines will be reviewed in early 2023, and the most up to date guidance can be found on the court’s website under “Court Operations and Schedules”, “Scheduling” and “Hearing Guidelines”. The general principles informing processes for hearing matters state that the default mode for matters that are more adjudicative/substantive in nature is an in-person hearing. The default mode for matters that are more administrative/procedural in nature is a remote hearing. The mode of hearing will be determined when a matter is scheduled and will depend on the availability of court resources on the hearing date. Changes to the mode of hearing after it has been scheduled must be approved by the Manager, Court Coordination. The following criteria will be considered when a change to mode of hearing is requested: • inability of a participant to attend in person due to health issues or other personal circumstances; • distance to the location of the hearing which makes in-person attendance impractical; • a change in the nature of the proceeding such as to necessitate a departure from the scheduled mode of hearing; • a change in representation of a party from self-represented to represented, or vice versa; and • such other reason as approved by the court. (Alta. Gaz. June 30, 2022)]

commentary.text:
Rule 6.9(1)(c) provides discretion to the court to make decisions based on the written record only: rule 6.9(1)(c). When the court exercises this discretion and uses a paper process, it is incumbent on the parties to put their “best foot forward” in the written materials. A key issue is whether a fair disposition can be made on the paper record, and if the parties believe that cannot be done an oral argument should be requested. (Alta. Q.B.).
Whether to permit oral argument is a matter of discretion, which will only be interfered with on appeal if the discretion is unreasonably exercised, or some manifest unfairness results.
Rule 6.9(2) confirms that many applications are within the jurisdiction of both applications judges (formerly styled “masters”) and judges. Where that is the case, and the hearing is in a judicial district where applications judges sit regularly, the application should be heard by an applications judge. NP#2016-10 (December 8, 2016).
By amendments to the Court of King’s Bench Act that came into force September 1, 2022, the titles of “master” and “master in chambers” were changed to “applications judge.” At hearings or in correspondence, applications judges should be addressed as “judge” or “your honour.” By Notice to the Profession and Public (with a revision dated November 25, 2016) the Court helpfully summarizes the jurisdictional law based on section 9(1)(a) of the Court of King’s Bench Act,  R.S.A. 2000, c. C-31. and lists  Carbone v. Dawes, [2023] A.J. No. 1374, 2023 ABKB 729 at paras. 98-99 (Alta. K.B.). applications under the and others Alberta Rules of Court under various statutes that may be heard by an applications judge. In general, clerks will re-direct any matters improperly set down in judges’ chambers to applications judges’ chambers or, where this is missed, the presiding judge will do so when the matter is spoken to.
The Notice also helpfully summarizes what applications judges may not hear, pursuant to section 9 of the Court of King’s Bench Act.85These include appeals, determination of disputed questions of fact, contempt and injunctions — as well as matters expressly required to be done by a judge.

data.title: Recording hearings when only one party present
data.text:
Unless the Court otherwise orders, a hearing of an application in which only one party makes a personal appearance must be recorded word for word by a method that is capable of providing a written transcript.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.13 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

data.text:

(3) An appeal from an applications judge’s judgment or order is an appeal on the record of proceedings before the applications judge and may also be based on additional evidence that is, in the opinion of the judge hearing the appeal, relevant and material.
(4) The record of proceedings is (a) the application before the applications judge, (b) affidavits and other evidence filed by the parties respecting the R. 6.13 (5) The appellant must file and serve on the respondent to the appeal, within one month after service of the notice of appeal, (a) any transcript of proceedings described in subrule (4)(c), (b) any additional evidence referred to in subrule (3), and (c) any further written argument.
(6) The respondent to the appeal must file and serve on the appellant, within R.S.A. 2000, c. C-15, s. 18(1). days after service of the documents referred to in subrule (5), (a) any further written argument the respondent wishes to make, and (b) any additional evidence referred to in subrule (3).
(7) The appellant may, within 10 days after service of the documents referred to in subrule (6), file a brief written argument responding to any unanticipated additional evidence or further argument raised by the respondent.
(8) A party may rely on its original written argument, if any, that was before the applications judge or any further argument filed under subrule (5)(c) or (6)(a), or both the original argument and the further argument.

data.title: Appointment for questioning under this Part
data.text:
If a party is entitled to question a person under this Part, that party may do so by serving on the person a notice of appointment for questioning in Form 29, and rules 6.16 [Contents of appointment notice]
[Form of questioning and transcript] to 6.20 apply.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.15 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

commentary.text: An appointment for questioning under Part 6 of the Rules is the means to compel a questioning (or cross-examination) on affidavit or questioning of a witness for purposes of an application. Consequences for failure to attend after proper service of proper appointment may include civil contempt: rule 10.52(3)(a)(iv).

data.title: Contents of notice of appointment
data.text:
(1) A notice of appointment for questioning must (a) specify a reasonable date, time and place for the appointment for questioning, (b) describe any records the person is required to bring to the appointment for questioning, and (c) request the person to be questioned to specify any arrangements necessary to accommodate the person’s reasonable needs which, to the extent reasonably possible, must be accommodated.
(2) The notice of appointment for questioning must be served 5 days or more before the appointment date (a) on the person to be questioned, or if a lawyer acts for that person, on the lawyer, and (b) on each of the other parties.
